Answer
rows: The process by which humans learn and internalise their culture’s norms and values.
It begins from the moment of birth and extends to the point of death.
Primary, secondary and tertiary socialisation.
The family.
Any four of: education, peer groups, the media, religion (the workplace is shown as tertiary on this site).
The workplace.
Formal: people are deliberately and consciously taught rules. Informal: people learn by watching and learning from others, unintentionally.
The social norms children learn at school without being officially or formally taught.
Labels or pet names used in the family that can teach gender expectations, such as ‘Princess’.
Guiding a child’s interests towards certain toys and activities, such as boys being encouraged to play football and girls to play house.
Social reactions to conformity (positive sanctions) or violation (negative sanctions) of the norms: rewards or punishments used to encourage conformity.
Formal, because it is given by an organisation (the school) with written rules.
Any one of: time-out at home, being left out of a group, ‘I’m very disappointed in you’.
The different processes through which society enforces conformity to the norms.
Norms are social rules and expectations about how people should behave. Values are shared ideas about what a group considers important, desirable or morally right.
Sewell.
